title: LLM
description: The brain behind ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. It read a mind-boggling amount of text and got really good at predicting what comes next, one little chunk at a time.
exercise: Ask it to explain LLMs using a hobby you love. Then explain it back and ask it to grade you.

title: Model vs. app
description: OpenAI is the company, GPT is the model and ChatGPT is the app you actually open. Same idea as Toyota, the engine and the Prius in your driveway.
exercise: Open the model picker in whatever app you use. Count how many models are hiding behind one app.
source: Our episode on the AI landscape

title: Prompt
description: Whatever you type or say to the AI. The good ones read less like a Google search and more like a text to a smart friend who has zero context on your life.
exercise: Ask the same thing twice. Once in five words, once with your goal and an example of a great answer. Compare.

title: Token
description: The bite-size pieces AI reads and writes in. One token is about three quarters of a word, which is why limits and prices get counted in tokens instead of words.
exercise: Paste a paragraph into OpenAI's tokenizer and watch it get chopped up. Emoji and long words are the fun ones.

title: Context window
description: How much the AI can hold in its head at once, including your messages, its replies and any files you drop in. Really long chats can push early details out, which is why they get forgetful.
exercise: When a long chat starts losing the thread, ask for a recap, start a fresh chat and paste the recap in.

title: Hallucination
description: When AI makes something up and says it with a straight face, like a quote nobody said or a study that doesn't exist.
exercise: Pick one fact from a chat, open the source it points to and see if the source backs it up.

title: Knowledge cutoff
description: The date an AI's built-in knowledge stops. Ask about anything after that and it's guessing, unless it can search the web.
exercise: Ask about something from this week with web search off, then turn it on and ask again.

title: Multimodal
description: AI that works with more than text. Show it a screenshot or send a voice memo and it can work with that too.
exercise: Snap a photo of your fridge and ask what you can make for dinner tonight.

title: Reasoning model
description: A model that takes a beat to work through a problem before it answers. Slower, but a lot better at math, planning and anything with a few moving parts.
exercise: Give the same brain teaser to the fast mode and the thinking mode. See which one falls for it.

title: Agent
description: AI you hand a goal instead of a question. It picks the steps, uses tools like search or your calendar, and keeps going until it's done or stuck.
exercise: Give an agent a small errand, like finding three dinner spots with a table for two on Friday. Watch what it does.

title: Automation
description: A fixed set of steps that runs the same way every time, like "when a receipt hits my inbox, save it to this folder." Unlike an agent, it doesn't make decisions along the way.
exercise: Write down one thing you do every week in the exact same steps. That's an automation waiting to happen.

title: Vibe coding
description: Building an app by describing what you want and letting AI write all the code. Andrej Karpathy coined it in February 2025, and Collins made it Word of the Year.
exercise: Ask an AI to build a one-page website for your dog. Don't touch a single line of code.

title: ChatGPT
description: The one everyone's heard of, and an easy first stop. Bring it a real task from your week instead of a test question.
exercise: Bring a decision you're stuck on and ask it to interview you before it gives any advice.

title: Claude
description: Anthropic's assistant. Josh leans on it for writing and building things, so it's the one he'll nerd out about.
exercise: Give Claude and ChatGPT the exact same task. Notice which answer you'd actually use.

title: Gemini
description: Google's assistant, and it shows up inside Gmail, Docs and Android. Handy if your life already runs on Google.
exercise: Ask it to find the last three emails about one plan and turn them into a to-do list.

title: Gemini Notebook
description: Google's research notebook. You give it your own sources and it answers from those, with citations you can click to check.
exercise: Add two articles that disagree on something. Ask where they agree and where they don't, then click the citations.

title: tldraw
description: A free whiteboard for sketching ideas and diagrams. Mary likes to start here whenever an idea needs to be a picture.
exercise: Sketch a process you know by heart. Ask AI to simplify the steps, then redraw it.

title: Granola
description: An AI notepad for meetings. It listens along, then turns your messy notes into clean ones once the call's over.
exercise: Use it on one low-stakes call and compare its notes to what you remember.

title: Wispr Flow
description: Talk instead of type, in any app. It's great for prompts, because people say way more out loud than they'd ever bother typing.
exercise: Next time you write a prompt, say it out loud instead and ramble a little. Compare the answer.

title: Projects
description: A folder for one ongoing thing, with its own chats, files and instructions, so you stop re-explaining your situation every single time.
exercise: Make a project for something you work on every week. Add your goal and one example of work you love.

title: Custom instructions
description: Standing notes the AI reads before every chat, like "I'm a beginner, skip the jargon" or "keep it short." Set them once and stop repeating yourself.
exercise: Write three lines about how you like answers. Paste them into your settings and see what changes.

title: Memory
description: When the app remembers things about you between chats, like that you're vegetarian or training for a marathon. Handy, and worth peeking at what it's saved.
exercise: Ask "what do you remember about me?" and clean up anything that's wrong or a little too personal.

title: Skills
description: Recipe cards for the AI. Each one is a set of instructions it pulls out only when a task calls for it, like "write in my voice" or "make a slide deck."
exercise: Pick a task you explain the same way every time and write the recipe down once.

title: Connectors
description: Plugs that let an assistant reach into your other apps, like your calendar, email or Google Drive, so it can work with your actual stuff. A lot of them run on MCP, an open standard for exactly this.
exercise: Connect one low-stakes app, like your calendar, and ask what your week really looks like.

title: Deep research
description: Ask a big question, go make a coffee, and come back to a cited report the AI pieced together from dozens of sources.
exercise: Have it research something you already know cold, then grade its homework.

title: Build one useful thing
description: Our standing challenge. Pick one annoying task from your week and get AI to help with it. Keep it small and real.
exercise: Decide what "done" looks like before you ask AI for anything.

title: Keeping up without drowning
description: You don't need every AI headline. A couple of sources you trust and a habit you actually like will get you way further.
exercise: Pick three words from this page you didn't know. Explain each one to a friend by Friday.

title: AI slop
description: The bland, over-polished stuff AI churns out when nobody edits it. You've seen the emails that open with "I hope this finds you well." We have opinions.
exercise: Paste something AI wrote for you and ask it to find every line that sounds like a robot.
source: The No AI Slop skill we use

title: Privacy and your data
description: What happens to the stuff you paste in? Worth five minutes in the settings before you upload your tax return.
exercise: Open the data settings in the AI app you use most and decide what you're comfortable sharing.

title: AI and energy
description: Every answer runs on a data center somewhere. How much power that takes, and whether AI ends up saving more than it uses, is still being worked out.
exercise: Skim the IEA's overview and sort what's measured today from what's a forecast.

title: AI and your job
description: Which parts of your work could get easier, which might change, and how you'd even tell. It depends a lot on the job.
exercise: List three things you did at work this week. For each, ask whether AI could do a first draft.

title: AGI
description: AI that can do most things a person can. Everyone defines it a little differently, so "how close are we?" turns into a pretty fun argument.
exercise: Find two definitions of AGI. For each, write down what would convince you we'd hit it.
